section.title: Arc length and surface area of revolution

introduction.p: Approximate a smooth curve by short line segments to compute its length. For a graph, the Pythagorean theorem gives the length factor \sqrt{1+(dy/dx)^2}. Rotating a short segment about an axis gives a surface-area contribution equal to circumference times segment length.

exercise.title: Why is a small piece of length slanted?

statement.p: A smooth curve is not a horizontal step dx. The small length is ds=\sqrt{(dx)^2+(dy)^2}. In your own words, why do short straight pieces come from the Pythagorean theorem, and why does that become \sqrt{1+\bigl(f'(x)\bigr)^2}\,dx for a graph?

hint.p: Each polygonal segment has a horizontal run and a vertical rise. Factoring out \Delta x turns the rise-over-run into a difference quotient, which approaches a derivative.

exercise.title: Why is arc length not the integral of |f'(x)|?

statement.p: Integrating |f'(x)| measures total vertical change. In your own words, why does that miss the length of even the line y=x from 0 to 1, and what extra motion does ds remember?

hint.p: A curve moves horizontally and vertically at the same time. Length needs both legs of the little right triangle, not only the vertical one.

hint.p: We are measuring the surface, not the solid inside it. Unwrapping the thin band produces circumference times arc length.

note.title: The lesson of arc length
note.p: The integral is not merely an antiderivative problem. It is a way to define and measure quantities. Some of those quantities require new functions or numerical approximation.

subsection.p: This chapter has asked what integrals measure. We have measured area, volume, mass, center of mass, work, hydrostatic force, average value, probability, length, and surface area.
The next question is computational.

exercise.title: Why can a natural length have no elementary antiderivative?

statement.p: The length of y=\sin x from 0 to \pi is a perfectly meaningful integral whose integrand has no elementary antiderivative. In your own words, why is the integral still a way to define and measure that length?

hint.p: Setting up an integral and evaluating it by an antiderivative are different jobs. A quantity can be exactly the value of an integral even when we must approximate that value.
